title: Cap. 1 subject: Tertio — rationality as common condition
latin: III. Tertio in loco jam accedamus ad qualitates sive conditiones subjecti communiter & indistincte considerati; hoc est, ad inquirendum, quibus qualitatibus necesse sit ut vestiatur, & quasi induatur illud subjectum, in quod hic actus Divinus sive praedestinationis sive reprobationis indiscriminatim terminetur. Primo, extra controversiam est, ut actus praedestinationis aut reprobationis cadat in subjectum quodcunque, hanc qualitatem sive conditionem requiri, ut illud subjectum sit natura rationali praeditum. Rationalitas ergo est necessaria conditio semper supponenda in subjecto vel praedestinato, vel reprobato. In promptu & cuivis obvia est hujus rei ratio; quia scilicet tam praedestinatio quam reprobatio est decretum Dei circa finem supernaturalem aeternae beatitudinis; cujus finis natura bruta nullo modo capax esse potest. Quando igitur dicimus aliquem ad beatitudinem ordinatum per praedestinationem, aut a beatitudine exclusum per reprobationem, necesse est ut utrumque de rationali creatura intelligatur. Sed quae perspicua sunt, longa esse non debent.
pass_a: III. In the third place let us now approach the qualities or conditions of the subject considered commonly and indistinctly; that is, unto inquiring by what qualities it is necessary that that subject be clothed, and as it were invested, into which this Divine act either of predestination or of reprobation is indiscriminately terminated. First, it is outside controversy that, in order that the act of predestination or reprobation fall upon any subject whatsoever, this quality or condition is required, that that subject be endowed with a rational nature. Rationality therefore is a necessary condition always to be supposed in the subject either predestined or reprobated. Ready at hand and obvious to anyone is the reason of this matter; because namely both predestination and reprobation is a decree of God concerning the supernatural end of eternal beatitude; of which end a brute nature can in no way be capable. When therefore we say someone ordered unto beatitude through predestination, or excluded from beatitude through reprobation, it is necessary that both be understood of a rational creature. But things that are clear ought not to be long.
pass_b: III. Third: the qualities or conditions of the subject taken commonly and without distinction — what must clothe that subject on which the Divine act of predestination or reprobation, taken without discrimination, terminates. First, beyond dispute: for either act to fall on any subject at all, that subject must be endowed with a rational nature. Rationality is therefore a necessary condition always to be supposed in the predestined or the reprobate. The reason is plain to anyone. Both predestination and reprobation are God's decree about the supernatural end of eternal blessedness, and brute nature cannot be capable of that end. So when we say someone is ordered to blessedness by predestination, or shut out of it by reprobation, both must be understood of a rational creature. What is clear need not be long.

title: Cap. 1 subject: sin-infection debated — Scotus / Suarez before foresight
latin: Est altera qualitas sive conditio quam plerique arbitrantur necessario prerequiri & praesupponi in actu Praedestinandi & Reprobandi, sed non est tam in confesso apud omnes: Haec autem est Peccati infectio, quam a Deo praevisam putant in subjecto, priusquam vel praedestinari vel reprobari possit. Ex horum igitur sententia, ut actus hi terminentur ad creaturam, non sufficit quod rationalis sit, sed etiam praesupponitur quod peccatrix, sive peccato coinquinata sit. Haud lubens hanc litem meam fecerim; paucis tamen quid ab aliis sentiatur, & quid ipse sentiam, aperiam. Est itaque nobis necessario fatendum, non esse nuper natam, aut ignobilium Theologorum sententiam, quae ponit praedestinationem priorem praevisione peccati. Imo omnes fere qui per praedestinationem intellexerunt non tam mediorum praeparationem, quam meram designationem ad ipsum finem, hoc modo philosophati sunt. Scotus ubi assignat ordinem instantium in mente & voluntate Divina, semper statuit priorem esse voluntatem dandi beatitudinem praevisione lapsus, Lib. 1. dist. 41. qu. unica; & lib. 3. dist. 19. qu. 1. ponit Deum in primo instanti voluisse gloriam determinato numero electorum, in secundo ordinasse illis gratiam, in tertio praevidisse eos lapsuros in Adamo. Jam cum dico Scotum in hac sententia fuisse, intelligitis & alios quam plurimos, qui Scotistae haberi volunt, idem sensisse. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonfus Mendoza, aliique innumeri decretum praedestinationis, non solum decreto lapsus permittendi, sed etiam hominis creandi, prius esse docent. Hi ergo non putant peccatum praevisum esse conditionem, aut qualitatem subjecti, in quod cadere debet actus praedestinationis. Postremo, ex Jesuitis neotericis, ipse Suarez hanc sententiam sequitur, & communem esse testatur, hisce verbis: Probabiliorem existimo communem sententiam Theologorum asserentium, electionem hominum praedestinatorum antecessisse permissionem originalis peccati.
pass_a: There is another quality or condition which most judge to be necessarily prerequisite and presupposed in the act of Predestinating and Reprobating, but it is not so much in confession among all: But this is the infection of Sin, which they think foreseen by God in the subject, before it can either be predestined or reprobated. From the opinion of these therefore, in order that these acts be terminated unto a creature, it does not suffice that it be rational, but it is also presupposed that it be a sinner, or stained with sin. Not gladly would I make this controversy mine; yet in a few words I will open what is thought by others, and what I myself think. It must therefore necessarily be confessed by us that that opinion is not recently born, or of ignoble Theologians, which places predestination prior to the foresight of sin. Indeed nearly all who through predestination understood not so much the preparation of means, as a mere designation unto the end itself, have philosophized in this mode. Scotus, where he assigns the order of instants in the Divine mind and will, always established the will of giving beatitude to be prior to the foresight of the fall, Book 1 distinction 41 unique question; and book 3 distinction 19 question 1 he places that God in the first instant willed glory for a determined number of the elect, in the second ordered grace for them, in the third foresaw them about to fall in Adam. Now when I say Scotus was in this opinion, you understand also that others as many as you will, who wish to be held Scotists, sensed the same. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonso Mendoza, and innumerable others teach the decree of predestination to be prior not only to the decree of permitting the fall, but even to that of creating the human being. These therefore do not think foreseen sin to be a condition, or quality of the subject, into which the act of predestination ought to fall. Finally, from the recent Jesuits, Suarez himself follows this opinion, and testifies it to be common, in these words: I judge more probable the common opinion of Theologians asserting that the election of predestined human beings preceded the permission of original sin.
pass_b: Another quality most writers treat as necessarily presupposed in predestinating and reprobating — though not all agree: the infection of sin, which they think God foresaw in the subject before it could be predestined or reprobated. On their view rationality is not enough; the creature must also be presupposed a sinner, stained with sin. I do not gladly make this quarrel my own; still I will open briefly what others hold and what I hold. We must admit that the opinion which puts predestination before foresight of sin is neither new nor the property of obscure theologians. Nearly everyone who took predestination as bare designation to the end itself, rather than preparation of means, reasoned this way. Scotus, ordering instants in the Divine mind and will, always set the will to give beatitude before foresight of the fall (I dist. 41; III dist. 19 q.1): God first wills glory for a fixed number of elect, next orders grace for them, then foresees their fall in Adam. With Scotus stand many who claim the Scotist name. Maclantus, Galatinus, Alfonso Mendoza, and countless others teach the decree of predestination prior even to permitting the fall — and prior to creating man. So they do not treat foresight of sin as a condition of the subject on which predestination falls. Among recent Jesuits Suarez follows the same line and calls it the common opinion: I judge more probable the theologians' common view that the election of the predestined preceded permission of original sin.

title: Cap. 1 subject: angels prove election before stand/fall; Thomas terminus
latin: Posse Deum eligere & reprobare ante omnem praevisionem peccati, manifestum est in Angelorum electione & reprobatione. Nam qui steterunt, proculdubio electi fuerunt; & qui ceciderunt, praeteriti sive reprobati, idque ante praevisum discrimen standi & labendi. Quod hac ratione ostendo. Necesse est ut concedamus, Deum intellexisse ante voluntarium decretum creandi aut salvandi Angelos, eos, quos tali gratia donaret, de facto in sanctitate perseveraturos, & aeternam beatitudinem adepturos; e contra, vidisse eos qui perierunt, infallibiliter casuros, si illam solam gratiam iis daret, quam de facto postea dedit. Quaero, Cur dedit bonis Angelis illam gratiam, quam sciebat illos ad gloriam perducturam? Aliud fingi non potest, nisi quod antecessit voluntas illos salvandi, quam appellamus Electionem vel Praedestinationem. Quaero itidem, Cur dedit malis illam gratiam, qua sola accepta intellexit illos infallibiliter perituros? Respondemus necesse est, Quia antecessit voluntas permittendi illos deficere a beatitudine: nam alioquin novit, & potuit Deus non minus illis quam aliis dedisse gratiam, quae infallibiliter eos provexisset ad gloriam. Videtis erga Angelos habuisse Deum voluntatem eligendi quosdam ad gloriam, & non eligendi alios, non ortam post praevisionem standi in his, labendi in illis; sed causam potius hujus discriminis & diversi eventus, ac proinde ordine priorem. Electio igitur & praeteritio non praesupponunt necessario ex ipsa natura actuum praevisionem peccati in subjecto; quia non in Angelis. Sed videtur etiam quod nec in hominibus necessarium est ponere praevisionem peccati, ut conditionem in subjecto praedestinato & reprobato, priorem ipso decreto Praedestinationis & reprobationis. Nam (ut recte annotavit Thomas) metus non accipit speciem a termino a quo, sed a termino ad quem. Sicut ergo nihil refert quantum ad rationem dealbationis, utrum ille qui dealbatus fuerit niger, aut pallidus, aut rubens; sic nihil refert ad rationem praedestinationis, utrum aliquis praedestinetur in vitam aeternam, a statu miseriae, vel non. Haec ille. Potest itaque (secundum Thomam) actus praedestinationis cadere in subjectum peccati miseria nondum implicatum.
pass_a: That God can elect and reprobate before every foresight of sin is manifest in the election and reprobation of Angels. For those who stood were without doubt elected; and those who fell were passed by or reprobated, and that before the foreseen discrimination of standing and falling. Which I show by this reason. It is necessary that we concede that God understood, before the voluntary decree of creating or saving Angels, those whom he would gift with such grace, that they would in fact persevere in holiness and obtain eternal beatitude; on the contrary, that he saw those who perished, that they would infallibly fall, if he gave them that grace alone which he in fact afterward gave. I ask, Why did he give to the good Angels that grace which he knew would lead them through unto glory? Nothing else can be invented, except that there preceded a will of saving them, which we call Election or Predestination. I ask likewise, Why did he give to the evil that grace which, alone having been received, he understood them infallibly about to perish? We must answer, Because there preceded a will of permitting them to fail from beatitude: for otherwise God knew, and was able no less to them than to others to have given grace which would infallibly have advanced them unto glory. You see that toward the Angels God had a will of electing certain ones unto glory, and of not electing others, not arisen after foresight of standing in these, falling in those; but rather the cause of this discrimination and diverse event, and therefore prior in order. Election therefore and passing by do not necessarily presuppose from the very nature of the acts the foresight of sin in the subject; because not in Angels. But it seems also that neither in human beings is it necessary to place foresight of sin as a condition in the predestined and reprobated subject, prior to the decree itself of Predestination and reprobation. For (as Thomas rightly annotated) motion does not take species from the terminus from which, but from the terminus unto which. Just as therefore it nothing matters as to the account of whitening, whether he who will have been whitened was black, or pale, or red; so it nothing matters to the account of predestination, whether someone is predestined unto eternal life from a state of misery, or not. These things he. The act of predestination can therefore (according to Thomas) fall upon a subject not yet implicated in the misery of sin.
pass_b: That God can elect and reprobate before any foresight of sin is plain in the angels. Those who stood were elect; those who fell were passed by or reprobated — and that before any foresight of standing versus falling. Before the decree to create or save them, God knew which angels, given such grace, would in fact persevere and reach eternal blessedness, and knew which would infallibly fall if given only the grace he later in fact gave. Why give the good angels grace he knew would bring them to glory? Only because a will to save them — election or predestination — came first. Why give the wicked angels grace he knew, taken alone, would leave them to perish? Because a will to permit their falling short of blessedness came first: otherwise he knew and could have given them, no less than the others, grace that would have carried them infallibly to glory. So toward the angels God's will to elect some and not others did not arise after foresight of who would stand or fall; it is rather the cause of that different outcome, and prior in order. Election and passing-by therefore do not, from the nature of the acts themselves, necessarily presuppose foresight of sin in the subject — not in angels. Nor does it seem necessary in humans to place foresight of sin as a condition in the subject prior to the decree of predestination and reprobation. Thomas notes rightly: motion takes its species from the terminus to which, not from the terminus from which. As whitening does not care whether the thing whitened was black, pale, or red, so predestination does not care whether someone is destined to eternal life from a state of misery or not. On Thomas's showing the act of predestination can fall on a subject not yet tangled in sin's misery.

title: Cap. 1 subject: Aquinas on reprobation/permission; Calvin not inventor
latin: Imo videtur Aquinas magis inclinare in illam sententiam, quae asserit ipsam reprobationem de facto antecessisse praevisionem originalis peccati. Nam cum dicit reprobare esse illam partem Divinae providentiae, quae permittit aliquos a fine beatitudinis deficere, innuit ipsam permissionem deficiendi a mediis ad beatitudinem ducentibus fluere a reprobatione, & proinde esse illa posteriorem secundum nostrum modum intelligendi. Quod si ipsa permissio deficiendi sequatur Reprobationem, tum multo magis praevisio actualis defectionis sive lapsus: praevidetur enim non nisi ex hypothesi permissionis. Haec a me in eum finem adducuntur, non quod huic sententiae adhaerescam, sed ut obiter perstringam illorum inscitiam dicam, an malitiam? qui Calvinum aut Bezam lacerant maledictis, quasi primarios autores hujus sententiae, quae inter Scholasticos & ipsos Pontificios non minus recepta est, quam illa contraria, quae ponit hominem peccato infectum subjectum praedestinationis. Atque ad Calvinum quod attinet, (quantum ego possum judicare) quamvis recte neget praescientiam peccati esse causam praedestinationis aut reprobationis; tamen cum Augustino semper statuit, praevisi peccati considerationem obversari Deo praedestinanti aut reprobanti, tanquam communem conditionem subjecti. Clara sunt illa verba, Si judicio mortis obnoxii sunt omnes naturali conditione, quos ad mortem Dominus praedestinat, si ex corrupta massa desumpti sunt omnes, non mirum si damnationi subjacent. Sed adhuc clariora audite. Postquam Paulus Deum ex perdita massa eligere & reprobare quos illi visum est, docuit, quare & quomodo id fiat adeo non expedit, ut potius expavescens in clamorem illum erumpat, O altitudo! Tract. De aeterna Dei praedestinatione, pag. 711. Scio Bezam, & Zanchium, aliosque viros perdoctos paulo durius loqui, & massae corruptae considerationem decreto praedestinationis omnino postponere, nunquam tamen damnationem alicujus decerni putant nisi ex praesupposito peccato.
pass_a: Indeed Aquinas seems more to incline into that opinion which asserts that reprobation itself in fact preceded the foresight of original sin. For when he says to reprobate is that part of Divine providence which permits some to fail from the end of beatitude, he hints that the permission itself of failing from the means leading unto beatitude flows from reprobation, and therefore is posterior to it according to our mode of understanding. Which if the permission itself of failing follows Reprobation, then much more the foresight of actual defection or fall: for it is foreseen not except from the hypothesis of permission. These things are adduced by me unto this end, not that I adhere to this opinion, but that in passing I may touch the ignorance — shall I say, or malice? — of those who lacerate Calvin or Beza with curses, as if primary authors of this opinion, which among the Scholastics and the Pontificians themselves is no less received than that contrary which places the human being infected with sin as the subject of predestination. And as to Calvin, (as far as I can judge) although he rightly denies foresight of sin to be the cause of predestination or reprobation; yet with Augustine he always established that the consideration of foreseen sin is set opposite to God predestinating or reprobating, as a common condition of the subject. Clear are those words, If by the judgment of death all are liable by natural condition whom the Lord predestines unto death, if from a corrupted mass all are taken, it is no wonder if they lie under damnation. But hear yet clearer ones. After Paul taught that God from a lost mass elects and reprobates whom it seemed good to him, why and how that is done so little profits, that rather growing terrified he breaks forth into that cry, O the depth! Tractate On the eternal predestination of God, page 711. I know Beza, and Zanchi, and other most learned men speak a little more harshly, and postpone altogether the consideration of the corrupted mass to the decree of predestination, yet they never think the damnation of anyone decreed except from presupposed sin.
pass_b: Aquinas even seems to lean toward saying reprobation in fact preceded foresight of original sin. When he calls reprobation that part of Divine providence which permits some to fall short of beatitude, he implies that permission to fail from the means that lead to beatitude flows from reprobation — and so, in our way of understanding, is posterior to it. If permission to fail follows reprobation, then foresight of the actual fall follows all the more: it is foreseen only on the hypothesis of permission. I bring this in not because I cling to that opinion, but to touch in passing the ignorance — or malice? — of those who curse Calvin or Beza as if they invented a view no less current among Scholastics and even Pontificians than the contrary view that puts the sin-infected human as predestination's subject. As for Calvin (so far as I can judge): he rightly denies that foresight of sin is the cause of predestination or reprobation; yet with Augustine he always holds that consideration of foreseen sin stands before God as he predestinates or reprobates — as a common condition of the subject. Clear words: If all whom the Lord predestines to death are by natural condition liable to death's judgment, if all are taken from a corrupted mass, no wonder they lie under damnation. Hear clearer still. After Paul taught that God from a lost mass elects and reprobates whom he wills, why and how so little helps that, terrified, he breaks into O the depth! (Tractate on God's eternal predestination, p. 711). Beza, Zanchi, and other learned men speak more harshly and set consideration of the corrupted mass wholly after the decree of predestination — yet they never think anyone's damnation decreed except on presupposed sin.

title: Cap. 1 subject: bare election vs means — Davenant's judgment
latin: Sed ut paucis expediam quid mei judicii sit hac in re. Primo, si per Praedestinationem quis intelligat solam designationem ad finem gloriae (sicuti multi intelligunt ex antiquioribus Scholasticis) & per Reprobationem solam negationem hujus actus, vel ipsum decretum praetereundi & non-eligendi, puto non esse necessarium ut supponamus peccatum fuisse praevisum in subjecto sic praedestinato aut reprobato, tanquam praecedaneum. Ratio haec est; Quia in actibus mentis & voluntatis Divinae unus non est realiter prior alio, sed tota haec prioritas & posterioritas desumitur ex mutua rerum dependentia: ubi ergo nulla est dependentia causalitatis inter res ipsas, nulla debet aut potest esse consideratio prioritatis aut posterioritatis in decretis Divinis, quae circa easdem versantur. Jam vero peccatum ad actum Divinae electionis vel non-electionis omnino impertinenter se habet: non est enim ratio actus sive hujus sive illius (ut omnes fatentur) neque est talis subjecti qualificatio, absque qua hi actus in subjectum cadere non possunt, sicuti est rationalitas; quod exemplo Angelorum antea demonstratum est. Cum itaque peccatum nec causa sit cur aliquis eligatur ad gloriam, aut permittatur deficere a gloria, nec dispositio subjecti sive ad hunc actum, sive ad illum necessaria, improprie loquitur, qui dicit hoc decretum eligendi aut non eligendi esse prius in mente Divina praevisione peccati; improprie etiam loquitur qui dicit praevisionem peccati fuisse priorem hoc decreto, cum inter res independentes nulla sit ponenda aut prioritas aut posterioritas, sive in mente, sive in voluntate Dei. Atque hinc colligere potestis, illos qui conantur horrendis nescio quibus consequentiis illorum sententiam deturpare, qui considerant decretum electionis & praeteritionis absque praevisione peccati, funiculos ex arena nectere.
pass_a: But that I may in a few words set forth what is of my judgment in this matter. First, if through Predestination someone understands sole designation unto the end of glory (just as many understand from the more ancient Scholastics) and through Reprobation the sole negation of this act, or the decree itself of passing by and not electing, I think it is not necessary that we suppose sin to have been foreseen in the subject thus predestined or reprobated, as something preceding. This is the reason; Because in the acts of the Divine mind and will one is not really prior to another, but this whole priority and posteriority is taken from the mutual dependence of the things: where therefore there is no dependence of causality among the things themselves, no consideration of priority or posteriority ought or can be in the Divine decrees which turn about the same. But now sin holds itself altogether impertinently toward the act of Divine election or non election: for it is not the reason of the act either of this or of that (as all confess) nor is it such a qualification of the subject without which these acts cannot fall upon the subject, as rationality is; which by the example of the Angels was demonstrated before. Since therefore sin is neither the cause why someone is elected unto glory, or permitted to fail from glory, nor a disposition of the subject necessary either unto this act or unto that, he speaks improperly who says this decree of electing or not electing is prior in the Divine mind to the foresight of sin; he also speaks improperly who says the foresight of sin was prior to this decree, since among independent things neither priority nor posteriority is to be placed, whether in the mind or in the will of God. And from this you can gather that those who try by I know not what horrendous consequences to defile the opinion of those who consider the decree of election and passing by without foresight of sin, are tying ropes from sand.
pass_b: My judgment in brief. First: if by Predestination you mean bare designation to the end of glory (as many older Scholastics do), and by Reprobation only the negation of that act — the decree to pass by and not elect — I do not think foresight of sin must be supposed as something prior in the subject so predestined or reprobated. Why? In God's mind and will no act is really prior to another; all before-and-after is taken from the mutual dependence of the things themselves. Where the things have no causal dependence, Divine decrees about them admit no before or after. Sin is altogether beside the point for the act of Divine election or non-election. It is not the reason of either act (all confess that), nor a qualification of the subject without which those acts cannot fall — as rationality is; the angels already showed that. Since sin is neither cause why someone is elect to glory or permitted to fall short of it, nor a disposition required for either act, it is improper to say the decree to elect or not elect is prior in God's mind to foresight of sin — and improper to say foresight of sin was prior to that decree — for among independent things there is no before or after in God's mind or will. Those who try to blacken, with I know not what horrid consequences, the view that considers election and passing-by without foresight of sin are twisting ropes out of sand.

title: Cap. 1 subject: Scripture sense — means & praedamnatio presuppose sin
latin: Veruntamen, quia sacra Scriptura, & decus Patrum Augustinus, videntur per praedestinationem & reprobationem, non meram & solam electionem ad finem, nec meram praeteritionem sive non-electionem ad talem finem intelligere, sed simul conjungere cum decreto dandi finem, decretum praeparandi & dandi certa, designata, & infallibilia media ad finem; & cum decreto permittendi aliquem deficere a fine, aliud decretum copulare, puniendi & in aeternum damnandi ipsum qui defecit; ob hanc, inquam, causam puto melius & commodius, addo etiam verius hoc sensu, praevisum peccatum praesupponi ut conditionem subjecti, in quod cadit decretum talis praedestinationis & reprobationis. Ad Scripturam quod attinet, per praedestinationem solet denotare non nudam designationem ad finem gloriae, sed destinationem ad gloriam per media; nec per media quaelibet, sed per media gratiae efficacis derivatae a Christo Capite & Mediatore nostro. Huc faciunt illa loca; Eph. i.4. Vos elegit in ipso ut essemus sancti. 2 Tim. i.9. Servavit nos ex suo proposito & gratia, quae data est nobis in Christo ante tempora secularia. Ex quibus locis, aliisque multis quae accumulari possent, perspicuum est, Apostolum per praedestinationem intelligere destinationem & directionem ad finem gloriae per infallibilia media gratiae efficacis a Christo derivandae. De Augustino notius est quam ut multis egeat, illum per praedestinationem designare praeparationem gratiae infallibiliter perducentis ad gloriam. Celebris est illa definitio, Praedestinatio est praeparatio beneficiorum Dei, quibus certissime liberantur, quicunque liberantur. Unde Aquinas describit praedestinationem esse actum providentiae specialis ordinantis & dirigentis electos ad finem salutis, non per media quaelibet, sed per talia quae ipsum eventum infallibiliter producent. Sumatur itaque hoc: Praedestinationem prout usurpatur in Scripturis, designare non decretum abstractum, de solo fine, sed decretum quasi complicatum, de dando fine vitae aeternae per media gratiae in Christo. Jam ad Reprobationem quod attinet, ex usu Scripturarum designat non nudam praeteritionem aut non-electionem, sed praedamnationem sive deputationem ad interitum, quae inseparabili nexu cohaeret cum non-electione sive praeteritione, saltem quoad eventum. Hoc inde patet, quod reprobati vocentur in Scripturis vasa irae coagmentata ad interitum, Rom. ix.22. Olim descripti ad damnationem, Judae 4. Et Augustinus reprobationem appellat praedestinationem ad interitum. Sub reprobationis itaque vocabulo comprehendere debemus non nudum decretum praetereundi, aut non-eligendi aliquos, sed insuper voluntatem illos praedamnandi. His positis, dico talem praedestinationem & reprobationem non recte concipi aut explicari posse, nisi praeconcepto peccato, ut communi conditione in ipso subjecto.
pass_a: Nevertheless, because sacred Scripture, and the glory of the Fathers Augustine, seem through predestination and reprobation to understand not mere and sole election unto the end, nor mere passing by or non election unto such an end, but at the same time to conjoin with the decree of giving the end, the decree of preparing and giving certain, designated, and infallible means unto the end; and with the decree of permitting someone to fail from the end, to couple another decree, of punishing and eternally damning him who failed; for this cause, I say, I think better and more fitting, I add also truer in this sense, that foreseen sin be presupposed as a condition of the subject, into which the decree of such predestination and reprobation falls. As to Scripture, through predestination it is accustomed to denote not bare designation unto the end of glory, but destination unto glory through means; nor through any means whatsoever, but through means of efficacious grace derived from Christ our Head and Mediator. Those places make for this; Ephesians 1:4. He elected you in him that we might be holy. 2 Timothy 1:9. He saved us from his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ before secular times. From which places, and many others which could be heaped up, it is clear that the Apostle through predestination understands destination and direction unto the end of glory through infallible means of efficacious grace to be derived from Christ. Concerning Augustine it is more known than that it needs many things, that he through predestination designates the preparation of grace infallibly leading through unto glory. Famous is that definition, Predestination is the preparation of the benefits of God, by which whoever are liberated are most certainly liberated. Whence Aquinas describes predestination to be an act of special providence ordering and directing the elect unto the end of salvation, not through any means whatsoever, but through such as will infallibly produce the event itself. Let this therefore be taken: that Predestination as it is used in the Scriptures designates not an abstract decree, concerning the end alone, but a decree as it were complicated, concerning giving the end of eternal life through means of grace in Christ. Now as to Reprobation, from the use of the Scriptures it designates not bare passing by or non election, but predamnation or deputation unto destruction, which coheres by an inseparable bond with non election or passing by, at least as to the event. This is plain from thence, that the reprobate are called in the Scriptures vessels of wrath fitted unto destruction, Romans 9:22. Formerly written unto damnation, Jude 4. And Augustine calls reprobation predestination unto destruction. Under the vocabulary of reprobation therefore we ought to comprehend not the bare decree of passing by, or of not electing some, but moreover the will of predamning them. These things having been posited, I say such predestination and reprobation cannot rightly be conceived or explained, unless sin having been preconceived, as a common condition in the subject itself.
pass_b: Yet Scripture and Augustine, glory of the Fathers, do not take predestination and reprobation as bare election to the end, or bare passing-by. With the decree to give the end they join the decree to prepare and give certain, designated, infallible means; with the decree to permit falling short of the end they couple another — to punish and damn forever the one who fell short. For that reason I judge it better, fitter, and in this sense truer that foresight of sin be presupposed as a condition of the subject on which such a decree of predestination and reprobation falls. In Scripture predestination usually means not bare designation to glory's end, but destination to glory through means — and not any means, but means of efficacious grace derived from Christ our Head and Mediator. So Ephesians 1:4: he chose us in him that we should be holy; 2 Timothy 1:9: he saved us according to his purpose and the grace given us in Christ before the ages. From these and many like them it is plain the Apostle means destination and direction to glory's end by infallible means of efficacious grace from Christ. Augustine, as everyone knows, takes predestination as preparation of the grace that leads infallibly to glory: Predestination is the preparation of God's benefits by which whoever are set free are set free with certainty. So Aquinas describes it as special providence ordering and directing the elect to salvation's end not by any means, but by means that produce the event infallibly. Take it thus: Predestination in Scripture is not an abstract decree about the end alone, but a compounded decree — to give eternal life through means of grace in Christ. Reprobation in Scripture's use is not bare passing-by or non-election, but pre-damnation — appointment to destruction — bound inseparably to non-election, at least as to the event. Scripture calls the reprobate vessels of wrath fitted for destruction ([[Romans 9:22 >> Bible:Romans 9:22]]); formerly marked out for condemnation ([[Jude 4 >> Bible:Jude 4]]). Augustine calls reprobation predestination to destruction. Under "reprobation" we must include not only the bare decree to pass by, but also the will to pre-damn. That kind of predestination and reprobation cannot be conceived or explained rightly unless sin is preconceived as a common condition in the subject.

title: Cap. 1 subject: reasons — Christ medicus; media; justice — common close
latin: Quod hisce rationibus ostendi potest. Primo, Praedestinatio hominum ad vitam aeternam continet in se donationem quorundam ipsi Christo, tanquam Medico aut Vivificatori; & exemptionem eorundem e stipite & capite veteris Adami, tanquam corruptoris & occisoris posterorum suorum. Huc spectant illa loca Scripturarum. Quos dedisti mihi, ego custodivi, Johan. xvii.12. Ecce ego & pueri quos dedisti mihi, Heb. ii.13. Elegit nos in Christo, Ephes. i.4. Non egent qui sani sunt medico, Luc. v.31. Christus cum adhuc infirmi essemus pro impiis mortuus est, Rom. v.6. Si unius delicto multi mortui sunt, multo magis gratia Dei, & donum per gratiam, quae est unius Jesu Christi, in multos redundavit, Rom. v.15. Ex hisce Scripturarum locis colligimus, In decreto praedestinationis omnes electos fuisse datos Christo ut Redemptori, ut Vivificatori, ut Medico eorundem futuro. At redemptor supponit captivum, vivificator mortuum, medicus aegrotum: ergo ut tales a Deo considerantur qui in Christo Redemptore praedestinantur. Nam ut quivis actus praesupponit objectum, sic talis actus tale objectum: actus igitur redemptionis, vivificationis, sanationis, qui omnes includuntur ut futuri in actu praedestinationis sive electionis nostrae in Christo, supponunt objectum redimendum, vivificandum, sanandum: quod nihil aliud est quam peccato corruptum. Hinc Augustinus, Serm. 9. De verb. Apost. Nulla causa fuit veniendi Christo Domino, nisi peccatores salvos facere. Tolle morbos, tolle vulnera, nulla causa est medicinae. Si Christus in tempore fuit incarnatus ut peccatores salvos faceret, tum etiam ab aeterno ut peccatores considerati sunt qui per praedestinationem Christo incarnando donabantur salvandi. Secundo, Praedestinatio non modo designat donationem quorundam Christo tanquam Redemptori & Liberatori, sed etiam praeparationem aeternam in mente Divina illorum mediorum per quae certissime liberentur. Ac omnia haec media, quae praeparantur electis, ejusmodi sunt quae propriam suam vim exercere nequeunt nisi circa subjectum peccato inquinatum: Tale igitur subjectum supponit praedestinatio. Nam ut ordinemur ab efficaci vocatione ad resipiscentiam & fidem: quis, quaeso, resipiscentiae usus nisi in homine peccatore? quae vis fidei nisi ad justificandum hominem peccatorem? quid facit spiritus regenerationis, nisi quod refingat peccatorem ad imaginem sanctitatis Divinae in Adamo amissam? Cum igitur praedestinatio haec aliaque ejusmodi media praeparet electis, manifestum est illos a Deo praedestinante considerari ut peccato corruptos, atque ex hac corruptione per media haec efficacia eruendos. Porro, quod ad reprobationem attinet, hoc unico argumento mihi videtur evinci, non cadere illam nisi in hominem consideratum ut peccatorem: Nimirum, quia scopus ejus est illustrare gloriam Divinam per modum vindicantis justitiae, sicuti scopus praedestinationis est illustrare gloriam Divinam per modum parcendi misericordiae. Non autem facit ad gloriam Dei illustrandam, si mente concipiamus illum destinasse poenae aeternae suam creaturam nondum poena dignam. Nam utcunque Deus, pro absoluta sua libertate, potest apud se decernere, quod creaturae, quantumvis innocenti, hoc aut illud bonum non sit communicaturus quod aliis communicabit, tamen non potest decernere, stante sua justitia, creaturae innocenti poenam infligendam. Quandoquidem ergo in reprobatione continetur voluntas inferendi poenam reprobato, necesse est ut ex hac parte Deo objiciatur ut peccato constrictus & contaminatus. Loquantur Scripturae, quae semper iram & vindictam Dei peccato provocatam docent: Tribulatio & angustia adversus omnem animam hominis perpetrantis malum, Rom. ii.9. Stipendium peccati mors, Rom. vi.23. Propter quae (id est, peccata sua) venit ira Dei super filios incredulitatis, Coloss. iii.6. Patres etiam universi solicite cavent, ne Deo tribuant voluntatem puniendi aut damnandi quemlibet, nisi ex occasione peccati praecedentis exortam. Tertullianus, De resurrect. Deus de suo bonus, de nostro justus. Intelligit justitiam vindicativam. Augustinus, potest Deus sine bonis meritis liberare, quia bonus est: non potest quenquam sine malis meritis damnare, quia justus est, Lib. 3. Advers. Jul. cap. 18. Prosper Ad Obj. Vincent. Respons. 2. Quod multi pereunt, pereuntium est meritum: quod multi salvantur, salvantis est donum. Et Respons. ad undecim, Ad praedestinationem Dei nihil aliud referri potest, nisi quod aut ad debitam justitiae retributionem, aut ad indebitam pertinet gratiae largitatem. Ex hisce omnibus quae disputata sunt, arbitror satis liquere, non modo rationalem naturam, sed peccatricem substare actui Divino sive praedestinationis sive reprobationis, tanquam communes subjecti conditiones, absque quibus neuter horum actuum posset in homines competere, eo modo quo praedestinatio & reprobatio in Scripturis describuntur.
pass_a: Which can be shown by these reasons. First, Predestination of human beings unto eternal life contains in itself the donation of certain ones to Christ himself, as to a Physician or Vivifier; and the exemption of the same from the stock and head of the old Adam, as of the corrupter and killer of his posterity. Those places of the Scriptures look hither. Those whom you gave me, I have guarded, John 17:12. Behold I and the children whom you gave me, Hebrews 2:13. He elected us in Christ, Ephesians 1:4. Those who are healthy do not need a physician, Luke 5:31. Christ, when we were still weak, died for the ungodly, Romans 5:6. If by the offense of one many died, much more the grace of God, and the gift through grace, which is of one Jesus Christ, abounded unto many, Romans 5:15. From these places of the Scriptures we gather, In the decree of predestination all the elect were given to Christ as Redeemer, as Vivifier, as their future Physician. But a redeemer presupposes a captive, a vivifier a dead one, a physician a sick one: therefore as such are they considered by God who are predestined in Christ the Redeemer. For as any act presupposes an object, so such an act such an object: the acts therefore of redemption, vivification, healing, which all are included as future in the act of our predestination or election in Christ, suppose an object to be redeemed, vivified, healed: which is nothing other than corrupted by sin. Hence Augustine, Sermon 9 On the words of the Apostle. There was no cause of the Lord Christ's coming, except to make sinners safe. Take away diseases, take away wounds, there is no cause of medicine. If Christ in time was incarnate that he might make sinners safe, then also from eternity those were considered as sinners who through predestination were being given to the incarnate Christ to be saved. Second, Predestination designates not only the donation of certain ones to Christ as Redeemer and Liberator, but also the eternal preparation in the Divine mind of those means through which they may most certainly be liberated. And all these means, which are prepared for the elect, are of such a kind that they cannot exercise their own proper force except around a subject stained with sin: Such a subject therefore predestination presupposes. For that we may begin from efficacious calling unto repentance and faith: what, I ask, is the use of repentance except in a sinful human being? what force of faith except unto justifying a sinful human being? what does the spirit of regeneration do, except that it reshapes the sinner unto the image of Divine holiness lost in Adam? Since therefore predestination prepares these and other such means for the elect, it is manifest that they are considered by God predestinating as corrupted by sin, and to be drawn out from this corruption through these efficacious means. Further, as to reprobation, by this sole argument it seems to me to be proven, that it does not fall except upon a human being considered as a sinner: Namely, because its aim is to illustrate the Divine glory by way of vindicating justice, just as the aim of predestination is to illustrate the Divine glory by way of sparing mercy. But it does not make for illustrating the glory of God, if in mind we conceive him to have destined to eternal punishment his creature not yet worthy of punishment. For however God, by his absolute liberty, can decree with himself that to a creature, however innocent, he is not about to communicate this or that good which he will communicate to others, yet he cannot decree, his justice standing, punishment to be inflicted on an innocent creature. Since therefore in reprobation is contained the will of inflicting punishment on the reprobate, it is necessary that from this side he be set before God as bound and contaminated by sin. Let the Scriptures speak, which always teach the wrath and vengeance of God provoked by sin: Tribulation and anguish against every soul of a human being perpetrating evil, Romans 2:9. The wages of sin is death, Romans 6:23. On account of which (that is, their sins) the wrath of God comes upon the sons of unbelief, Colossians 3:6. The Fathers also universally carefully guard, lest they attribute to God a will of punishing or damning anyone, except one arisen from the occasion of preceding sin. Tertullian, On the resurrection. God is good from his own, just from ours. He understands vindicative justice. Augustine, God can liberate without good merits, because he is good: he cannot damn anyone without evil merits, because he is just, Book 3 Against Julian chapter 18. Prosper To the Objections of Vincent Response 2. That many perish is the merit of those perishing: that many are saved is the gift of the one saving. And Response to the eleven, Unto the predestination of God nothing else can be referred, except what pertains either unto the due retribution of justice, or unto the undue largess of grace. From all these things which have been disputed, I judge it sufficiently clear that not only a rational nature, but a sinful one underlies the Divine act either of predestination or of reprobation, as common conditions of the subject, without which neither of these acts could compete upon human beings, in that mode in which predestination and reprobation are described in the Scriptures.
pass_b: That can be shown by these reasons. First: predestination of humans to eternal life includes giving certain ones to Christ as Physician and Life-giver, and freeing them from the stock and head of old Adam, corrupter and killer of his posterity. So Scripture: "Those you gave me I have kept" ([[John 17:12 >> Bible:John 17:12]]); "Behold, I and the children God has given me" ([[Hebrews 2:13 >> Bible:Hebrews 2:13]]); "He chose us in Christ" ([[Ephesians 1:4 >> Bible:Ephesians 1:4]]); "Those who are well have no need of a physician" ([[Luke 5:31 >> Bible:Luke 5:31]]); "While we were still weak, Christ died for the ungodly" ([[Romans 5:6 >> Bible:Romans 5:6]]); "If many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many" ([[Romans 5:15 >> Bible:Romans 5:15]]). From these we gather: in the decree of predestination all the elect were given to Christ as Redeemer, Life-giver, and their future Physician. But a redeemer presupposes a captive, a life-giver a dead person, a physician a sick one — so those predestined in Christ the Redeemer are considered by God as such. As any act presupposes an object, such an act presupposes such an object: the acts of redemption, vivification, and healing, all included as future in our predestination or election in Christ, presuppose an object to be redeemed, made alive, healed — which is nothing other than one corrupted by sin. So Augustine (Serm. 9 on the Apostle's words): There was no cause for the Lord Christ's coming except to save sinners. Take away diseases and wounds, and medicine has no cause. If Christ was incarnate in time to save sinners, then from eternity too those given by predestination to the incarnate Christ to be saved were considered as sinners. Second: predestination means not only giving some to Christ as Redeemer and Liberator, but also the eternal preparation in God's mind of the means by which they are most certainly set free. All those means prepared for the elect can exercise their proper force only on a subject stained with sin — so predestination presupposes such a subject. Begin with efficacious calling to repentance and faith: what use is repentance except in a sinner? what force has faith except to justify a sinner? what does the Spirit of regeneration do but reshape the sinner to the image of Divine holiness lost in Adam? Since predestination prepares these and like means for the elect, God clearly considers them corrupted by sin and to be drawn out of that corruption by those efficacious means. As for reprobation, one argument seems enough: it falls only on a human considered as a sinner. Its aim is to display Divine glory by way of vindicating justice, as predestination's aim is to display that glory by way of sparing mercy. It does not serve God's glory to conceive him as destining to eternal punishment a creature not yet worthy of punishment. By absolute liberty God may decree not to communicate to an innocent creature some good he will give others; yet standing in his justice he cannot decree to inflict punishment on an innocent creature. Since reprobation includes the will to inflict punishment on the reprobate, on that side the person must be set before God as bound and stained by sin. Scripture always teaches wrath and vengeance provoked by sin: tribulation and anguish on every soul that does evil ([[Romans 2:9 >> Bible:Romans 2:9]]); the wages of sin is death ([[Romans 6:23 >> Bible:Romans 6:23]]); because of these (their sins) the wrath of God comes on the sons of disobedience ([[Colossians 3:6 >> Bible:Colossians 3:6]]). The Fathers carefully refuse to attribute to God a will to punish or damn anyone except as arising from preceding sin. Tertullian (On the resurrection): God is good from his own, just from ours — meaning vindicative justice. Augustine (Against Julian 3.18): God can free without good merits, because he is good; he cannot damn anyone without evil merits, because he is just. Prosper (Reply to Vincent's objections 2): That many perish is the merit of those perishing; that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. And in the Reply to the eleven: Nothing can be referred to God's predestination except what belongs either to due retribution of justice or to undue largess of grace. From all this I judge it clear enough: not only a rational nature but a sinful one underlies the Divine act of predestination or reprobation — as common conditions of the subject without which neither act can fall on humans in the way Scripture describes those acts.
